resources.string: Rest the phone across the record weight, over the spindle, so its centre of mass sits on the axis
The phone’s bottom edge faces you (as if it were lying flat on a table)
Screen up, with the record weight resting on the platter’s own felt mat

A phone sitting off to one side slows the platter and amplifies the wobble — measured, 0.3% slower with a once-per-revolution wobble a third bigger. Centring is the least trouble: nothing to counterbalance with, and the phone lies flatter.

No record weight? That works too: put the midpoint of the phone’s right long edge against the spindle with the body on the left half, then place something of equal weight opposite it (a small mug filled with water does nicely), about the same distance from the spindle.
Placed this way, the text on the measuring screen also faces you the right way up.
1×/rev — eccentricity (platter, spindle or belt contact surface off-center)
2×/rev — an out-of-round platter, or two-point wear on the spindle. But if the 1×/rev above is large, this is most likely just its harmonic: bring the eccentricity down first, then look again.
Slower than one revolution — belt circulation, or a long-period drift
Non-harmonic (%1$.1f× the platter) — a part of the drive chain; a candidate for the motor or a pulley
2×/rev — out-of-round platter (most likely just a harmonic when 1× is large)
Slower than one revolution — belt cycle

That figure is the deck\'s error multiplied by the gyroscope\'s. Calibration uses a stopwatch and only has to be done once per phone. Wow & flutter and the other percentages are unaffected — those work without calibration.
The full explanation is under “About” on the main screen.
Not enough data for this metric yet — a trend needs at least two measurements.
Hollow points are uncalibrated runs. Their error is the deck\'s error multiplied by the gyroscope\'s, so it cannot be compared with calibrated points.
Hollow points are uncalibrated runs — but this metric is a ratio, unaffected by calibration, so it is still comparable.
Practically unchanged from the first run.
%1$s by %2$.3f percentage points compared with the first run (%3$.3f%% → %4$.3f%%).

Frequency on the horizontal axis (logarithmic, Hz), amplitude on the vertical (%). Orange dots are integer harmonics of the platter — things turning with it; grey dots are not, and belong to drive-chain parts turning at other speeds.
The largest error is at %1$.0f° (the pointer). Colour concentrated on one side means eccentricity; spread evenly means random flutter.

Angles cannot be compared between runs. 0° is wherever the platter happened to be the instant you tapped Start, and that is random. To compare, put a mark on the platter and always wait until the mark reaches the same place (say, the tonearm side) before you start.
The colour scale was expanded to fit the maximum — when comparing with another run, read the numbers on the legend rather than the shades.

Raw, unsmoothed error in %. The pale band is the min-to-max of each slice (fast flutter); the solid line is the mean of the same slice (slow drift). The analysis path never applies a moving average — smoothing carves out the flutter around 4 Hz and makes the numbers meaninglessly pretty. The compression here affects only the picture, never any number.
No measurements yet. Each finished analysis is saved here automatically — there is no Save button to remember.
%1$d in all, newest first. None of the percentages depend on calibration (they are ratios, so the gyroscope\'s scale-factor error cancels out); only RPM does.
%1$.1f s of unsteady speed was trimmed off
This run was not calibrated, so its error cannot be used to adjust the deck — it is the deck\'s error multiplied by the gyroscope\'s, and the two cannot be separated.
e.g. after adjusting the speed trimmer, from cold, at 45 RPM
Write down what you did this time. Three months from now a column of numbers only tells you something changed, not why.
This device has no gyroscope and no gravity sensor, so it cannot measure.

This device has no gyroscope. Not every Android phone does — mid-range models often leave it out.\n\nThis app measures rotation rate with the gyroscope; without one there is no way to measure, and neither the accelerometer nor the magnetometer can stand in. Please use a phone that has a gyroscope.
This device has no gravity or accelerometer reading, so it cannot measure.
The run was too short — only %1$d samples were recorded.
The speed was never steady during the whole run. Was the platter actually spinning? At least 5 continuous seconds are needed.
Only %1$.3f RPM was measured — the platter was not spinning.
Not enough data to analyze. Try measuring for longer — 90 s or more is more reliable.
The previous calibration is no longer valid
That calibration was done on a %1$s; this is a %2$s. The factor is tied to one particular gyroscope and cannot carry over. Please calibrate again.
You need one completed measurement first, so there is a reading to compare against. Go back, measure once, then return here.
k = %1$.3f is implausible. A MEMS gyroscope\'s scale-factor error is on the order of a few percent,
never this far off — check whether the revolution count or the seconds were mistyped.

1. Stick a visible mark on the edge of the platter\n2. Start the stopwatch and start counting as the mark passes a fixed reference point\n3. Stop when the mark passes the same point after the set number of revolutions

100 revolutions at 33⅓ takes about 3 minutes and gives ±0.17%; 200 revolutions about 6 minutes and ±0.08%.\nToo few revolutions is not worth doing — 10 gives only 1.7%, barely better than no calibration at all.
Measure twice as usual: once with just the phone, once with something of known weight stacked on top of it. Then pick those two runs below.

Both runs must have the same balance, with only the mass changing — so the phone goes centred on the record weight and the extra mass stacks directly on top of it. Adding mass to an off-centre phone changes the imbalance, not the load, and the slope comes out wrong.
This test needs at least two saved measurements. Measure twice as described above first.
A kitchen scale is precise enough for the added weight — any error just scales the slope proportionally.
There is no turntable profile yet, so the result has nowhere to go. Add one under “Turntable profiles” first.
Pick two different runs and enter the added weight.
The phone’s weight does affect the reading.
This deck is insensitive to load — the phone’s weight does not affect the reading.
Enter the revolutions and seconds and the factor is calculated.
The stopwatch has to time the same stretch of rotation. If you adjusted the speed or changed speed settings partway through, this k is wrong.
The slope is within measurement noise — this deck is insensitive to load, so the phone’s weight does not affect the reading.
The phone\'s weight %1$s the platter by %2$.4f RPM (%3$.3f%%). That is a bias of the measurement method, not a fault of the deck — the true unloaded speed is %4$.4f RPM.
Once the factory spec and drive-chain dimensions are recorded, results are compared against the spec automatically and non-harmonic peaks can be matched to real parts.
Fill this in and the analysis page will show exactly how far your deck is over spec. Manuals usually quote it as WRMS or DIN.
Platter diameter where the belt runs

Fill these in and the “non-harmonic ×N” peaks in the spectrum can be matched to real parts — the peak that lands right on the drive ratio is the motor. Measure the outer rim if the belt runs there, the sub-platter if it runs inside.

Belt thickness moves the ratio a lot: with an 8.5 mm pulley and 0.5 mm of belt, the thickness alone shifts it by 5.6%. Rough measurements are fine — the app always states the expected and the measured figure side by side rather than passing a match/no-match verdict.
Whether the phone’s weight slows your deck depends entirely on the motor type — no table can tell you, you have to measure it.
e.g. belt replaced in 2026; speed trimmer is on the right of the base plate

The phone turns with the platter, so what it measures is the speed of the platter. Pitch variation caused by an off-centre record hole is completely invisible to this method — and in practice that is often the largest single component of the wow you actually hear.
In other words: a pretty number here does not guarantee steady playback. It tells you how good the deck itself is, not how good this particular record will sound.

A gyroscope can have a fixed proportional reading error. It is multiplicative and never averages out, no matter how long you measure — only an external reference can remove it. This app uses a stopwatch: put a mark on the platter, time 100 revolutions, work out the true speed and compare it with the app\'s reading.
Until you calibrate, the error % cannot be used to adjust the deck — what you see is the deck\'s error multiplied by the gyroscope\'s, and the two cannot be separated.

Wow & flutter and every other percentage are unaffected, though: they are ratios, so the gyroscope\'s scale-factor error cancels out exactly. The diagnostics therefore work without calibration; calibration only affects “is my deck running at the right speed”.
A calibration belongs to this one device (every phone\'s gyroscope differs) — switch phones and it has to be redone.
Much of the reported eccentricity is the phone, not the deck

A phone sitting on the platter is itself an off-centre mass and generates its own once-per-revolution disturbance. Measured on the deck this app was developed with: more than half of the reported 1× came from the phone, not the turntable.

To find out how much is the deck\'s own: measure once, rotate the phone 180° in place, measure again. The phone\'s contribution flips phase and the deck\'s does not, so the difference between the two runs is the phone\'s share.
By the same token, if the 1×/rev is large, the 2×/rev below it is most likely just its harmonic rather than an out-of-round platter — bring the eccentricity down first, then look again.

• Centre the phone (see the placement diagram) — this matters most
• Level the deck, and the phone with it
• Measure at least 90 s; spectral resolution is 1 ÷ measurement length
• For accurate peak amplitudes measure 3 minutes — a 1-minute run underestimates by
 about 8%, because the resolution is too coarse and the peak falls between two bins
• Run the stopwatch and the app on the same stretch of rotation when calibrating
• Do not touch the deck or the table while measuring
Take off magnetic accessories and cases with magnets in them. A magnet near an MC cartridge can damage it permanently.
Lock the tonearm into its rest; never leave the cartridge hanging over the platter. If it meets the phone while the phone is on the platter, it is the stylus that loses.

Felt, non-woven or rubber mats all work; you do not need to put a record down as well. What matters is not pressing the phone straight onto the bare platter — that scratches both. Check the back of the phone and the mat for grit first.
At 78 rpm keep it near the centre: the centrifugal force on an off-centre placement is 5.5× what it is at 33 rpm.

The phone sits on the spinning platter and the gyroscope measures its rotation rate. The three-axis rate is projected onto the direction of gravity, so a slightly crooked placement does not affect the reading — a 5° tilt read on a single axis would underestimate by 0.38%, already past the accuracy target.

On Android the requested sample rate is only a hint; the actual rate is up to the vendor\'s implementation. Timestamps therefore always come from the sensor\'s own clock, no interval is assumed equal, and the data is resampled to a uniform grid before analysis. What you actually got is shown under “Sampling diagnostics”.
Measurement data stays on this device and is never uploaded anywhere.
This device lacks a gyroscope or gravity sensor and cannot measure.
Tap the button, then put the phone on the platter. Recording only starts once the speed is steady, and ends automatically when the platter stops.
You start and stop it yourself. Remember to get the platter spinning and the phone placed before you tap Start.
Before you put it on the platter
Not calibrated yet. The “error %” you see is turntable error multiplied by gyroscope error; the two cannot be separated, so it is not usable for adjusting your deck.
Speed is not steady yet, or outside the nominal range
No significant periodic component found — that is good news: no single part dominates the error.
Integer multiples = something turning with the platter (eccentricity, distortion). Non-integer = a part of the drive chain running at a different speed (motor, pulley).
Matches this deck’s drive ratio (%1$.1f×) — this is the motor.
This deck’s drive ratio is %1$.1f×; the measured order is %2$.1f× (%3$+.0f%%) — either the drive-chain dimensions are a little off, or this peak is not the motor.
Take off magnetic accessories and cases with magnets, and lock the tonearm down.

Rest the phone across the spindle on the record weight so its centre of mass sits over the axis — that is the least trouble. Without a record weight, put the midpoint of the phone\'s right long edge against the spindle with the body on the left half, and counterbalance with something of equal weight opposite.

A phone off to one side slows the platter by 0.3% and swells the once-per-revolution wobble by a third. Measurements show most of that 1×/rev comes from the phone, not the deck — to find the deck\'s own share, rotate the phone 180° and measure again; the difference is the phone\'s contribution.
Factor k = %1$.5f, applied to every speed reading.

This run\'s per-sample data has been saved as JSON (timestamps, rotation rate, gravity vector). Copy it to a computer and re-analyse it with tools/analyze_export.py, or compare it against another measuring tool.
Measure at least 90 s; for accurate peak amplitudes make it 3 minutes — a 1-minute run underestimates by about 8%, because the resolution is too coarse and the peak falls between two bins.
Unsteady stretches were skipped automatically: %1$.1f s at the start, %2$.1f s at the end. Every number below comes from what remains.

On Android the requested sample rate is only a hint; the actual rate is up to the vendor\'s implementation. You can run this with the phone lying still — sampling behaviour has nothing to do with whether the platter turns.

The timestamps are honest (%1$.3f%% off the wall clock) — a rate above what was requested just means the sensor runs faster, which is harmless here because integration always uses the real timestamps.

⚠ The timestamps differ from the wall clock by %1$.2f%% — every frequency-domain result shifts by the same amount, the order readings on the peaks cannot be trusted, and the time base has to be corrected first.
The timestamp ratio only means something after 10 s (the dispatch delay of the first event is magnified over a short span).
iOS baseline (iPhone 15 Pro Max): median 9.990 ms, std. dev. 0.005 ms, jitter 0.05%, worst gap 1.00×

The two sections below are automatic-calibration attempts that have been proven to fail; they are kept for diagnostics only. The only calibration you can trust is the stopwatch calibration on the main screen.
Not one full revolution yet — no factor can be computed.
Not one full revolution yet — no factor can be computed.

The two paths differ by only %1$.0f°, below the %2$.0f° noise floor — this factor cannot be trusted.\n\nWhile the platter spins fast the system weights the magnetic correction down to almost nothing and the bearing degenerates into the gyroscope integral itself. In that state “the gyroscope is accurate” and “the bearing is the gyroscope integral” are indistinguishable; the data simply does not contain that information.
The two paths genuinely diverge, so this factor means something. Relative precision %1$.3f%%.

The local field overwhelms the geomagnetic one and the circle no longer encloses the origin — the angle can only swing back and forth, so this path does not hold. Remove magnetic accessories and cases with magnets first; the geomagnetic horizontal component in Taiwan is about 37 µT, and anything larger than that breaks it.
Not enough samples to fit a centre yet, or the run is still going. The circle fit is computed once, after you stop.
The residual is far smaller than the radius — this data really is a circle.

The residual is the same order as the radius — this data is not a stable circle and the result cannot be trusted. The cause is the spatial gradient of stationary magnetic sources in the room; move the phone and it comes out completely different.
Uncalibrated magnetometer (independent of the system\'s bias estimate)
Total angle after removing the centre

The system\'s bias estimator keeps altering the calibrated field reading during a run. The uncalibrated raw reading is shown alongside it here: if the two k values differ a lot, that estimator is the disturbance.
Remove magnetic accessories and cases with magnets, lock the tonearm, and rest the phone on the platter’s own mat (or on a record weight).
